abstract: Plant intraspecific chemodiversity drives plant-herbivore and -pollinator relationships in plots, but whether it also impacts other members of the canopy arthropod community remains unclear. Furthermore, little is known of how different spatial components of plot intraspecific chemodiversity; chemical composition of individual plants within plots (i.e. -chemodiversity); differences in chemical composition among plants within plots (i.e. {beta}-chemodiversity); and cumulative chemical composition of all individuals in plots (i.e. {gamma}-chemodiversity), impact aboveground community assemblage. Using a chemodiversity field experiment containing 84 plots each planted with different combinations of Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare L., Asteraceae) chemotypes (i.e. a manipulated gradient of plot-level chemotype richness), we investigated the effect of plot-level chemodiversity and its components on the diversity and composition of canopy-associated arthropod communities within plots. We found significant impacts of the presence of certain chemotypes on the effective number of common arthropod taxa (Hill q = 1) and the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Importantly, the observed pattern was independent of the actual terpenoid (-)chemodiversity of these chemotypes. We also found that plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) reduced the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots, driven by impacts on dominance of a nematoceran species associated with Tansy. Cumulative plot terpenoid richness ({gamma}-chemodiversity) did not significantly impact arthropod communities. Instead, we observed that increased terpenoid abundance negatively influenced the effective number of common (Hill q = 1) and dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Our results suggest that within plants of the same species, the chemotypic identity of plants and presence within plots and plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) may impact arthropod communities by selecting for specific arthropod taxa making arthropod communities less even. Our results emphasize the nuanced impacts of chemodiversity at different levels and highlight taxon-specific arthropod responses.
